facts.note: Header note: the ModernGov URL / PDF filename says '2025-26' but the paper itself is titled 'TREASURY MANAGEMENT MONITORING 2026/27' at the top of p.1 and reports April–May 2026 figures throughout. Treat as 2026/27 Q1. Very thin document by design — no CFR, no maturity ladder, no liability benchmark, no MRP discussion (the Council does not borrow), no adviser named.

facts.value: TIES — zero on zero. `python3 monitor/outreach/price_book.py --find "Ribble Valley"` returns 'no borrower matching Ribble Valley'; the same is true of `--find "Ribble"`. The paper (§7.4) states outright: 'The council does not currently hold any long-term loan debt.' And §7.6: 'No temporary loans were taken out in the current financial year up to the 31st May 2026, or in the same period during 2025.' Zero PWLB in our file, zero borrowing in the paper — the two agree.

facts.value: Debt-free on both a long-term and a short-term basis for the whole reporting period. §7.4: no long-term loan debt. §7.6: no temporary loans in 2026/27 to 31 May, or in the same period during 2025. IFRS 16 finance-lease impact deferred to year-end (footnote under §8.5 table).
facts.note: The paper carries an Authorised Limit of £8,398k and Operational Boundary of £2,566k for 2026/27, but Actual at 31 May 2026 is £0. Utilisation of the Authorised Limit is 0.0%. IFRS 16 leases 'will be reported at year end as an outturn position' — figure not disclosed in this monitor.

facts.value: £18,715k at 31 May 2026: £18,100k of fixed-term deposits (100% DMO) plus £615k call cash held with HSBC (banking provider). Down from £25,500k at 1 April 2026 (net movement -£7,400k). Monthly balances: Mar-26 £23.8m, Apr-26 £23.1m, May-26 £18.7m — DMO carries virtually the entire book throughout.
facts.note: Two live tickets at 31 May: £16,500k @ 3.71% (26/05–01/06) and £1,600k @ 3.735% (28/05–22/06). Annex 1 shows twelve DMO tickets across April–May 2026, every one placed with the DMO, tenor 3–25 days, rates in a 3bp band from 3.705% to 3.735%. No use of any of the seven approved banks or six approved building societies for fixed-term investment in the period.

facts.value: £132,606 actual to end May vs £131,330 budget = £1,276 favourable variance. Full-year budget (£787,980) at assumed average 3.72%. Same period in 2025: £171,158 (higher base rate then).
facts.note: Principal-weighted average rate on the twelve Apr–May DMO tickets (Annex 1) works out at 3.713%, within a fraction of a basis point of the paper's 3.72% budget assumption. Budget-setting has landed almost exactly. Full-year phasing check: 61/365 of (£787,980) = (£131,724); the paper's two-month budget of (£131,330) sits £394 from a flat pro-rata, so the phasing is roughly linear.

facts.value: Authorised Limit for external debt 2026/27: £8,398k. Operational Boundary: £2,566k. Actual at 31 May 2026: £0. Utilisation: 0.0%. IFRS 16 finance leases 'will be reported at year end as an outturn position' — not included in this figure.
facts.note: Investment maturity ceiling (§8.6): policy is not to invest for periods longer than 365 days. No investment in the period ran beyond one year. No maximum-investment-beyond-one-year upper limit is set because none of the book qualifies.

summary.text:
Ten-page Q1 monitoring report to the 16 June 2026 Policy & Finance Committee, covering only the first two months of 2026/27 (1 April to 31 May 2026). Marked INFORMATION. Ribble Valley is a small debt-free district: §7.4 states outright that 'the council does not currently hold any long-term loan debt' and §7.6 confirms no temporary loans in the period. Our loan file returns no PWLB entries for Ribble Valley under any casing, so the reconciliation ties zero on zero — the strongest form the cross-check can take for a council in this position. No CFR, no maturity ladder, no liability benchmark, no MRP discussion; the paper is not that shape of document. IFRS 16 lease impact is deferred to the year-end outturn (§8.5 footnote), so the balance-sheet identity is not fully checkable here.

The distinctive thing is the investment posture. At 31 May 2026 the book stood at £18,715k — £18,100k of fixed-term deposits (100% DMO) plus £615k of HSBC call cash (banking provider). Monthly balances: Mar £23.8m, Apr £23.1m, May £18.7m — DMO carries virtually the whole book throughout. Annex 1 lists twelve tickets across April–May 2026, every one placed with the DMO, tenors 3–25 days, rates in a 3bp band from 3.705% to 3.735%. None of the seven approved banks or six approved building societies received a fixed-term deposit in the period; the approved list is on the shelf. Investment income for the two months was £132,606 against a phased budget of £131,330 — a £1,276 favourable variance — and the budgeted full-year average of 3.72% is landing almost exactly against the actual principal-weighted 3.713% on the Apr–May tickets.

The paper's dated view on interest rates is worth noting. §5.1 cites the BoE April 2026 Monetary Policy Report's market-implied path: Bank Rate rising to 4.20% by early 2027 before gradually falling to 4.00% by early 2028. §5.2 frames Middle East conflict as an upside skew, and §12.2 concludes 'it is possible that the Bank of England's base rate will begin to increase during this financial year, which will in turn increase the interest rates available on fixed-term deposits.' The reference period-end Bank Rate is 3.75%, and the MPC's April 2026 vote was 8-1 to hold (§10.2). This is a testable, dated position on rates from the paper's own text.

officer.body:
Hi [FIRST NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO curve, and a training academy for officers and members. More — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Monitoring report that went to Policy & Finance Committee on 16 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The budget-to-actual on your rate assumption is unusually tight, which is what made this worth writing.

A cross-check first, which comes out cleanly. Our loan file returns no PWLB entries for Ribble Valley, and the paper agrees — paragraph 7.4 states outright that the Council does not currently hold any long-term loan debt, and paragraph 7.6 confirms no temporary borrowing in the period or in the same period during 2025. Zero on zero is the strongest form the loan-book cross-check can take for a council in your position, and it means the Authorised Limit of £8.4m at paragraph 8.5 is entirely precautionary headroom.

The distinctive thing on the other side is the shape of the investment book. Every one of the twelve fixed-term tickets in Annex 1 sat with the DMO — twelve deposits across April and May, tenors of three to twenty-five days, rates in a three-basis-point band from 3.705% to 3.735%. Of the councils we've read, very few run a fixed-term book that sits exclusively with the DMO; more typically the approved list of banks, building societies and other local authorities is used alongside it. Your paragraph 9 approved list carries six top-tier building societies and seven UK clearing banks that meet your F2 minimum, and the LA market and MMFs are also inside your framework. We're not saying anything about whether that mix is right for a treasury run at Ribble Valley's scale — the DMO trade-off is genuine (Government-guaranteed collateral against the yield forgone), the counterparty framework you have in place clearly works, and this is a small district where operational simplicity is a real consideration. It is however the shape that most stands out about the book to a reader coming to it fresh.

And it is landing where the budget was set. Your assumed average of 3.72% for 2026/27 (paragraph 4.3) sits within a fraction of a basis point of the principal-weighted 3.713% average of the twelve Apr–May tickets, and your two-month variance of £1,276 on £131,330 (paragraph 4.4) is remarkably tight for eight weeks in. Not every budget-setting call we read lands that well.

One last thing worth noting from the paper's own text. Paragraph 5.1 cites the Bank of England's April Monetary Policy Report market-implied path — Bank Rate rising to 4.20% by early 2027 before falling to 4.00% by early 2028 — and paragraph 12.2 concludes 'it is possible that the Bank of England's base rate will begin to increase during this financial year, which will in turn increase the interest rates available on fixed-term deposits.' That is a dated, falsifiable position of the sort we watch across the library, because market-implied paths move quickly and it is useful to know how a council's own printed view sits against where the curve has since travelled. Our daily rate page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard carries the whole PWLB curve at both fixings; the SONIA forward curve and OIS view sit alongside it and are the most direct read on how the deposit end has repriced against what the paper prints.

One standing thing worth mentioning: our liability benchmark pathway is interactive and built on live data, which matters given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. Your paper quite properly doesn't carry a benchmark — the Council doesn't borrow — but the pathway is useful for understanding how peers set the ratio you'd sit above if the capital programme ever moved you into borrowing, at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit. DMADF deep dive is the obvious one given the shape of Annex 1. Term deposits, CDs & T-Bills covers the sector-wide toolkit alongside it. Mid-year & quarterly reporting is written for exactly the shape of report you produce for Policy & Finance. And Reading the quarterly & outturn reports is a members' course written for the committee this goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
